array.name: flatten / flat
array.example:
arr.flat()  // one level
arr.flat(Infinity)  // full flatten

array.name: sort (immutable)
array.example:
arr.toSorted((a, b) => a - b)
arr.toSorted((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b))
array.notes: Non-mutating; prefer over [...arr].sort(). .sort() mutates in place. helpers4/array provides sortNumberAscFn / sortStringAscFn as reusable comparator shortcuts — they are excluded from the native-alternatives rule

array.name: sortBy / orderBy
array.notes: Immutable version of .sort(); helpers4/array provides createSortByStringFn/NumberFn/DateFn/NaturalFn comparator factories for object arrays, and sortStringNaturalAscFn for human-friendly ordering of strings with embedded numbers

array.name: union
array.notes: Compose helpers4/array unique with spread; no dedicated helper needed

array.name: select / filterMap
array.notes: Two-pass but readable; no performance issue at typical array sizes

number.name: min / max
number.notes: For large arrays, prefer reduce to avoid stack overflow

number.name: ceil / floor
number.notes: No precision param natively; use roundTo from helpers4 for decimal precision

number.name: toInt / toFloat
number.notes: Radashi adds default-value fallback on NaN

object.name: merge (shallow)
object.notes: For deep merge, use mergeDeep from helpers4

map.name: forEach
map.notes: Not implemented — native Map.prototype.forEach already has this exact (value, key, map) signature, nothing to add.

map.name: reduce / some / every
map.example:
map.entries().reduce((acc, [k, v]) => acc + v, 0)
map.entries().some(([k, v]) => v > 10)
map.notes: Iterator Helpers make these one-liners on map.entries()/.values() — but the callback receives a [key, value] tuple to destructure every time. helpers4/map's versions take (value, key) directly, matching Map.prototype.forEach's own argument order, so they're still provided.

map.name: findKey / findValue
map.example:
map.entries().find(([k, v]) => v > 10)?.[0]  // key
map.entries().find(([k, v]) => v > 10)?.[1]  // value
map.notes: Composable via Iterator Helpers' .find(), but needs a tuple destructure plus an optional-chained index every call site — helpers4/map's versions are still provided for that reason.

map.name: hasValue
map.notes: Thin wrapper for readability — Map.prototype.has() checks keys, not values, which is the actual reason this needs its own name.

map.name: groupBy
map.notes: Map.groupBy groups into arrays of matching entries (multiple items per key) — not the same as countBy (counts per group) or the classic keyBy idea (single last-write-wins item per key, implemented here as toMapByKey — see that function's own docs for why it's not named keyBy). Deriving either from Map.groupBy's output is a real extra step, so both remain genuinely useful.

set.name: forEach
set.notes: Not implemented — native Set.prototype.forEach already covers this.

set.name: reduce / some / every / find
set.example:
set.values().reduce((acc, v) => acc + v, 0)
set.values().find(v => v > 10)
set.notes: Not implemented — unlike Map (whose entries are [key, value] tuples needing a destructure), Set already iterates plain values with no shape mismatch against these native methods. There's no real convenience left to add over calling them directly on set.values().

set.name: map / filter
set.example:
new Set(set.values().map(v => v * 2))
new Set(set.values().filter(v => v > 0))
set.notes: Iterator Helpers give the transform; reconstructing a Set from the result is the part still worth a named helper for.

set.name: groupBy
set.notes: Same distinction as helpers4/map's countBy/toMapByKey: Map.groupBy groups into arrays, it doesn't count or index-by-last-write.

set.name: union
set.notes: Landed natively as of the Set methods proposal — also .isSubsetOf() / .isSupersetOf() / .isDisjointFrom(). Not implemented here; native coverage is already complete for set-algebra operations.

set.name: intersection
set.notes: Landed natively as of the Set methods proposal — also .isSubsetOf() / .isSupersetOf() / .isDisjointFrom(). Not implemented here; native coverage is already complete for set-algebra operations.

set.name: difference
set.notes: Landed natively as of the Set methods proposal — also .isSubsetOf() / .isSupersetOf() / .isDisjointFrom(). Not implemented here; native coverage is already complete for set-algebra operations.

set.name: symmetricDifference
set.notes: Landed natively as of the Set methods proposal — also .isSubsetOf() / .isSupersetOf() / .isDisjointFrom(). Not implemented here; native coverage is already complete for set-algebra operations.

type.name: isNaN
type.notes: Prefer Number.isNaN() over global isNaN() which coerces

type.name: isFinite / isFiniteNumber
type.notes: Prefer Number.isFinite() over global isFinite() which coerces

type.name: isInfinite
type.notes: Number.isFinite() is the complement; compose with a NaN guard if needed. No dedicated helper warranted.

type.name: isSet (Set data structure)
type.notes: Not implemented to avoid confusion with the former isSet (now isDefined)

random.name: uid
random.notes: Generates UUID v4; Radashi uid is shorter and customizable. For UUID v7, use uuid7 from helpers4/math

random.name: uuid
random.notes: UUID v4 only; for UUID v7 (sortable, timestamped) use uuid7 from helpers4/math

date.name: toTemporalInstant
date.notes: Converts a Date to Temporal.Instant. Available without a flag since Node 26 (first LTS with Temporal enabled by default).

date.name: toPlainDate / toPlainDateTime / toPlainTime
date.notes: Extracts date-only or time-only from a ZonedDateTime

date.name: now (date/time/instant)
date.notes: Replaces new Date() for Temporal contexts

date.name: from (parse temporal string)
date.notes: Each Temporal type has a static .from() method for strict parsing

date.name: add / subtract (date arithmetic)
date.notes: Works on PlainDate, PlainDateTime, ZonedDateTime, Instant. Duration can be object or Temporal.Duration

date.name: until / since (difference)
date.notes: Returns a Temporal.Duration; available on all Temporal date/time types

date.name: compare (ordering)
date.notes: Static method on each Temporal type; returns -1, 0, 1 — ideal for .sort()

color.name: lighten / darken
color.since: CSS Color 5 (Baseline widely available since 2023 — Chrome 111, Firefox 113, Safari 16.2)
color.notes: CSS-only — only usable inside a CSS property value (inline style / stylesheet), not callable as a plain JS function and not available in Node. A JS helper is still useful for non-DOM contexts (SSR theming, CLI tools, backend color logic).

color.name: withAlpha (change the alpha channel of an existing color)
color.since: CSS Color 5 relative color syntax (Baseline widely available since September 2024 — Chrome 119+)
color.example: background: rgb(from lime r g b / 50%);
color.notes: CSS-only, same caveat as color-mix() above — not a JS-callable function, unavailable in Node.

color.name: isLight / isDark (pick a readable text color)
color.since: CSS Color 6 (Baseline newly available since April 2026 — Chrome 147, Firefox 146, Safari 26.0)
color.notes: CSS-only and very recently shipped, so real-world support is still limited. Picks black/white for you but does not expose a numeric contrast ratio — a JS contrastRatio()/isLight() helper remains useful for Node/non-DOM contexts and for anything needing the actual WCAG number.
